abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

sections.body: The paper names two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with task diversity. It groups tasks by shared capability requirements rather than surface modality, and builds a capability tree from verified trajectories. Three roles couple world generation with Harness evolution. Creator builds simplified worlds for each node, Explorer evolves reusable modules on a Harness tree, and Evolver organizes tasks and consolidates updates. A capability-aware router then selects compatible module configurations. The stated contributions are capability-driven recursive self-improvement, capability–module priors checked by controlled interventions, and transfer to unseen and real-world embodied tasks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Manual Harness iteration and costly environment construction limit multimodal agents, so The Trinity evolves Harnesses along shared capability requirements.

sections.body: A Harness coordinates a frozen model through six protocols: Perception, Memory, Inference, Planning, Orchestration, and Loop. Each protocol takes public observations, history, and controller state, and produces facts, a memory view, candidate options, a directive, available resources, and an execution and commitment. Modules are pure functions of supplied public records, and only Memory may declare explicit carry. Capabilities and protocols have a many-to-many relationship: the capability tree groups shared requirements, while protocols locate module updates. Evaluation-time skills are prepared separately and are not stored, evolved, inherited, or routed in the tree.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Long-horizon multimodal tasks depend on a Harness of six control protocols that coordinate a frozen model.

sections.body: Evolver normalizes benchmarks into specifications of goals, observations, actions, feedback, completion criteria, and budgets, grouped into five requirement domains. Capability categories are proposed from training tasks only, and a prefix trie over sorted requirement sets forms the capability tree. Creator builds simplified worlds for each node, and Explorer admits only worlds within a predefined intermediate-performance band. Explorer evolves local modules and inherits parent modules only when the updated parent has strictly higher host-verified performance. Routing uses public task information and verified experience, with retrieval at cosine similarity ≥ 0.5 and a 20,000-record FIFO memory.
sections.heading: The Trinity
sections.headline: The Trinity builds a capability tree from training trajectories and evolves Harness modules in verified simulated worlds.

sections.body: The experiments test capability-driven organization, iterative self-improvement, capability-aware routing, capability–module relations, and embodied transfer. In the organization comparison, Capability-Domain reaches 49.25/39.43 on Train/Unseen and Capability Tree (Sim) reaches 56.95/47.26, with first-iteration training costing 405.70M tokens for Sim. From Base to Iteration 4, Unseen rises from 42.1 to 64.1. Full self-routing scores 71.27 on Train and 60.96 on Unseen, against Oracle's 73.16 and 63.61. Adding a relevant module raises the Base score from 39.06 to 58.45. On embodied tasks, SOON reaches 80% in simulation and 60% on the robot with the final Harness.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Across 28 training and 18 unseen benchmarks, mean Train score rises from 39.1 to 73.2 by Iteration 4.

sections.body: Prior harness self-improvement methods adapt harnesses per task family, per task, or on the task stream, and include typed primitives and regime-branched trees. Trinity differs by inducing a capability tree from training trajectories, sharing prefixes across 44 heterogeneous benchmarks with selective module inheritance, and evaluating on held-out benchmarks and real robots. For agent–environment co-evolution, the section identifies SPADE as closest: one LLM designs environments with verification code and learns roles by reinforcement learning. Trinity keeps the backbone frozen and routes among capability-specific Harnesses.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work covers harness self-improvement and agent–environment co-evolution, where Trinity induces a capability tree from trajectories.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the position that capability requirements should organize Harness evolution. Creator's simplified, verifiable worlds provide execution feedback that guides module evolution, and the resulting Harness configurations specialize by capability. Controlled interventions and capability–module correlations are presented as empirical support for using capability requirements as priors for module design. Capability-aware routing selects suitable configurations from public task information and verified experience. The authors report improved aggregate performance on diverse training and unseen benchmarks, and transfer to two real-world embodied settings.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Capability-driven self-improvement with capability-aware routing improves aggregate performance and transfers to two real-world embodied settings.

sections.body: The authors state two limitations. Retrieval coverage and result quality for web-search benchmark discovery may vary across queries. The current study also focuses primarily on self-improvement at the Harness level. The outlook proposes dynamically expanding the capability tree to capture emerging requirements, and extending capability-driven learning to model parameter training. In that extension, capability-aware routing and self-improvement would form a closed loop that jointly drives capability discovery, acquisition, and refinement.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The stated limitations are web-search benchmark discovery and a focus on Harness-level self-improvement only.

sections.body: Core contributors are Weidong Tang, Ruiheng Wang, Jingxuan Zhang, and Hexin Wang. Additional contributors are listed by name, with affiliation numbers. Corresponding authors are Pengfei Zhou, Odin Zhang, and Yang You. The affiliations are InfRec, Xidian University, Tongji University, National University of Singapore, University of California, Berkeley, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, The University of Hong Kong, and Shanghai Innovation Institute.
sections.heading: Authors
sections.headline: The author section lists core contributors, contributors, three corresponding authors, and nine affiliations.

sections.body: Appendix A describes 44 benchmarks in five domains and 15 subclasses, with 26 training, 16 unseen, and two embodied benchmarks. Appendix B gives six capabilities and 30 defect types, and the capability tree paths. Appendix C and D describe the Explorer tree of 29 modules and the Creator library of 25 modules, along with the frozen Claude Opus 5 backbone and evaluation protocol. Appendix E describes embodied environments, which use one level per node and iteration, giving 44 levels, and compares Base and evolved Harness behavior on SOON and CaP-X.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix describes the task tree, capability and Harness trees, evaluation details, and per-benchmark decision figures.
